safetyNote: Poisonous: do not eat. Amanita regalis is listed for the panther cap poisoning syndrome, associated with ibotenic acid and muscimol. Symptoms can include vomiting, confusion, hallucinations and altered consciousness. Cooking did not fully neutralize its toxins in a published three-patient poisoning report. If ingestion is suspected, contact a poison centre or medical service promptly and retain any specimens.

sections.title: Brown cap and veil fragments
sections.text: The cap starts rounded and expands to a broad, glossy brown disc, usually about 10–20 cm across. Cream to pale yellow remnants of the universal veil form irregular warts or patches, often roughly concentric; heavy rain may wash them away. The mature margin can become slightly grooved. The flesh is pale and does not redden when cut; a golden-yellow layer immediately beneath the cap skin is described in detailed accounts.

sections.title: Gills, ring and bulb
sections.text: The crowded gills are free from the stem, white when young and sometimes pale yellowish later. The robust, pale stem has a hanging, grooved membranous ring. Its enlarged basal bulb bears several concentric bands of pale yellowish, scaly volval remnants, rather than a neat free cup in mature specimens. The whole stem base should be examined: its bands may remain informative when the cap warts have washed away. The spore deposit is white.

sections.title: Habitat and lookalikes
sections.text: Amanita regalis forms mycorrhizae with trees, especially spruce and birch, and fruits in woodland mainly from late summer into autumn. It is widespread in Scandinavia and also reported from parts of eastern Europe. Brown forms of Amanita rubescens can resemble it, but the latter reddens when damaged. Amanita pantherina has a different, more sharply rimmed basal bulb. None of these single differences is safe as the sole basis for deciding edibility.

sections.title: Documented poisoning
sections.text: The German Society for Mycology places A. regalis in its Pantherina syndrome group with A. muscaria and A. pantherina; it names ibotenic acid and muscimol and gives a typical latency of 15 minutes to four hours. In a published report, three people mistook A. regalis for parasol mushrooms: all developed substantial nausea and vomiting after one to two hours, while two also had neurological or cholinergic symptoms. All three recovered, but the report specifically found that cooking did not completely neutralize toxicity. Severity can vary, so any suspected ingestion needs professional advice.

traits: Broad glossy brown cap, usually 10–20 cm, with cream to pale yellow removable veil warts
Crowded free white gills, sometimes pale yellowish with age; white spore deposit
Pale robust stem with a hanging, grooved membranous ring
Swollen bulb carrying concentric bands of yellowish scaly volval remnants
Pale flesh that does not redden; golden-yellow layer directly beneath the cap skin
Mycorrhizal mainly with spruce and birch; northern and eastern European woodland
